lab_title: Retrograde Motion: From Puzzle to Heliocentric Insight
top_level_objectives: Understand why outer planets appear to reverse direction in the night sky over time
Recognize that retrograde motion is an optical illusion caused by relative orbital motion, not a true reversal
Compare the heliocentric model's elegant explanation of retrograde motion to the geocentric model's awkward epicycles
Observe how the retrograde effect varies with planetary distance from the Sun

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce students to the observational reality of retrograde motion as ancient and medieval astronomers encountered it, setting up the puzzle that drove cosmological change.
key_visuals: Night sky view from Earth showing Mars drifting eastward through constellations
Time-lapse sequence showing Mars slowing, reversing into a westward loop, then resuming eastward motion over several months
Zodiacal constellation backdrop with Mars's path traced as a looping line
Calendar or date markers showing the ~26-month cycle
student_actions: Observe Mars's motion night by night across the star field
Identify the point where Mars begins to slow and reverse
Sketch or trace the looping path Mars traces against the background stars
Note the timeframe of the entire retrograde event (roughly 2 months of backward motion)

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how the geocentric model attempted to explain retrograde motion through epicycles, illustrating the mechanical complexity that made astronomers question the model.
key_visuals: Earth at center of a model solar system
Mars on a large circular orbit (deferent) around Earth
A small circular orbit (epicycle) attached to Mars, causing it to trace a looping path
Animated motion showing how the epicycle creates the retrograde loop
Comparison text noting the increasing complexity as more planets required epicycles
student_actions: Watch the epicycle animation and trace Mars's path relative to the fixed Earth
Identify how the epicycle motion creates the retrograde loop
Discuss (or answer) why adding epicycles feels ad hoc or inelegant as an explanation
Observe how similar epicycles would be needed for other planets

scenes.scene_name: The Heliocentric Viewpoint: Outside the Solar System
scenes.brief_purpose: Transition to the Sun-centered perspective and show how retrograde motion emerges naturally from Earth and Mars orbiting at different speeds—setting up the key insight.
key_visuals: Bird's-eye view from far above the solar system plane
Sun at the center
Earth's orbit (inner, blue) and Mars's orbit (outer, red) drawn as circles or ellipses
Earth and Mars as labeled spheres in their respective orbits
Orbital motion animated to show Earth moving faster than Mars
A line of sight from Earth toward Mars and beyond to a distant star field
student_actions: Examine the orbital geometry and identify which planet orbits closer to the Sun
Note the relative speeds: Earth orbiting faster on its smaller inner orbit, Mars orbiting slower on its larger outer orbit
Predict what will happen over time as Earth gradually catches up to Mars
Relate the orbital speeds back to Kepler's laws if applicable

scenes.brief_purpose: Animate the heliocentric system through a retrograde event, showing the moment when Earth overtakes Mars and how this relative motion appears as a reversal from Earth's viewpoint.
key_visuals: Heliocentric orbital view with Sun, Earth, and Mars
Time markers showing passage of days/weeks
A 'line of sight' beam projected from Earth toward Mars and the background stars
Mars's position on the background star field updating in real time as the viewpoint sweeps
Arrows or labels indicating Earth's faster orbital motion and Mars's slower motion
Visual highlighting when Earth is closest to Mars and moving fastest relative to it
student_actions: Play the animation and watch Earth gradually catch up to and pass Mars
Observe how the line of sight from Earth to Mars sweeps backward (westward) against the background stars during the overtaking
Identify the moment of closest approach and fastest relative motion
Predict what should happen to the retrograde loop if Earth were moving even faster or Mars even slower

scenes.brief_purpose: Display both reference frames simultaneously during a retrograde event, showing that both describe the same phenomenon but reveal the true cause only in the heliocentric frame.
key_visuals: Split or dual view showing the night sky from Earth on one side and the heliocentric orbital diagram on the other
Mars's looping path traced in the left panel (geocentric view)
Earth and Mars's smooth orbital motion in the right panel (heliocentric view)
Synchronized animation so both views show the same moment in time
Annotations linking specific moments (e.g., 'closest approach') across both perspectives
student_actions: Compare the two views frame by frame as the retrograde event unfolds
Identify which view reveals the simple cause (heliocentric relative motion) and which masks it (geocentric looping)
Discuss why the heliocentric explanation is more parsimonious
Make predictions about what would change if Earth's or Mars's orbit were different

scenes.scene_name: Comparative Retrograde: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn
scenes.brief_purpose: Show how retrograde loops vary in size and duration for different outer planets, demonstrating that planetary distance determines the magnitude of the relative-motion effect.
key_visuals: Three side-by-side night-sky views showing retrograde loops for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn simultaneously
Mars loop: moderate size and duration (~2 months, moderate arc across the sky)
Jupiter loop: smaller and shorter (~1 month, tighter arc, farther from Sun's influence)
Saturn loop: even smaller and shorter (~4 weeks, tightest arc, slowest orbital motion)
Heliocentric diagrams for each planet showing orbital radius, orbital speed, and relative positions
Data or text annotations showing orbital periods and distances
student_actions: Observe the three retrograde loops and note how size and duration decrease with increasing distance from the Sun
Relate loop size back to the heliocentric model: farther planets move slower, so Earth's overtaking effect is less dramatic
Calculate or estimate relative orbital speeds if provided with orbital data
Explain why Jupiter's loop is smaller than Mars's using the heliocentric framework

scenes.brief_purpose: Reinforce understanding through a familiar everyday analogy—passing a car on a highway—showing that retrograde motion is the same optical illusion happening in the solar system.
key_visuals: Split view: a highway scene showing two cars, with one car passing the other
Your car (representing Earth) on the inside lane, moving faster
The other car (representing Mars) on the outside lane, moving slower
From your car's perspective, the other car appears to drift backward during the pass
Animation of the passing event
Diagram overlaying the car analogy onto the Mars retrograde event, labeling correspondences (your car = Earth, other car = Mars, relative velocity = apparent backward drift)
student_actions: Watch the highway passing scenario and note the apparent backward motion of the other car
Relate this to retrograde motion: Earth is the faster car, Mars is the slower car, and the night sky is the landscape
Discuss why the analogy works and what 'appears backward' means in both contexts
Extend the analogy: what if your car were going even faster? What if the other car were going faster than yours?

scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate learning by having students revisit the historical puzzle with their new heliocentric understanding and reflect on how a shift in perspective solved a centuries-old mystery.
key_visuals: Montage of key images from earlier scenes: geocentric epicycles, heliocentric orbits, night-sky loops, the highway analogy
Timeline or historical markers showing the transition from geocentric to heliocentric astronomy
A final unified diagram showing both the apparent motion (retrograde loop) and the true motion (smooth heliocentric orbits)
student_actions: Revisit the initial retrograde observation and explain it using the heliocentric model
Compare the elegance and simplicity of the heliocentric explanation to the geocentric epicycles
Summarize the key insight: retrograde motion is not a property of Mars's actual motion, but an illusion of relative motion from Earth's perspective
Discuss why this shift in perspective was so difficult for astronomers to accept and why empirical observation eventually forced the change
